note: Synthetic hand-written submissions with expected category outcomes, for smoke-testing a JudgeConfig before field scoring (issue #10). Not real projects, never part of a field or PoolArtifact. 'eligible' is compared with the code-computed two-of-three gate; 'min'/'max' bound the three-run criterion means. Only the categories listed under 'expect' are scored.

controls.purpose: Real gameplay: documented objective, rules, win and loss states

submission.name: Lantern Drift
submission.tagline: Guide a paper lantern through a storm before its flame goes out.
submission.inspiration: We wanted a short browser game that is tense but calm to look at.
submission.what_it_does: Lantern Drift is a 2D browser game. The player steers a lantern with the arrow keys through five storm levels. Gusts push the lantern sideways and rain shrinks its flame; collecting sparks refills it. You win a level by reaching the shrine at the top and lose when the flame reaches zero.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used Phaser 3 with TypeScript. Each level is a Tiled map; a wind system applies random gust forces every few seconds, and an arcade-physics overlap check handles spark pickups and the flame meter.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Gusts felt unfair at first, so we added a one-second warning streak before each gust.
submission.accomplishments: All five levels are playable from the title screen to the win screen, with a restart on loss.
submission.what_we_learned: Playtesting with friends changed our level layouts more than anything else.
submission.whats_next: Add a level editor and an online leaderboard.

controls.purpose: Unity/VR without gameplay: no objective, rules or player challenge

submission.name: CampusVR
submission.tagline: Walk the UCF campus in virtual reality before your first day.
submission.inspiration: New students get lost during their first week on a large campus.
submission.what_it_does: CampusVR is a virtual reality tour. Users put on a Quest headset, walk between five campus buildings and open floating info panels with office hours and room numbers.
submission.how_we_built_it: We built the scenes in Unity with the XR Interaction Toolkit, imported building models from SketchUp and wrote C# scripts for teleport movement and the info panels.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Large building models dropped the frame rate on the headset, so we simplified the meshes.
submission.accomplishments: The walkthrough of all five buildings runs on a Quest 2.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned how to profile and optimize Unity scenes for standalone VR.
submission.whats_next: Add more buildings and voice-guided directions.

controls.purpose: AI product: a trained model drives the core user-facing feature

submission.name: LeafLens
submission.tagline: Snap a tomato leaf and get a disease diagnosis in seconds.
submission.inspiration: A teammate's family garden lost its tomato crop to early blight last summer.
submission.what_it_does: Users photograph a tomato leaf in the web app. A computer vision model classifies it as healthy or one of six diseases, shows the confidence and highlights the infected region with a heatmap.
submission.how_we_built_it: We fine-tuned a MobileNetV2 image classifier in PyTorch on the PlantVillage tomato images, exported it to ONNX and serve it from a FastAPI endpoint. Grad-CAM produces the heatmap shown in the React front end.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Photos taken outdoors looked different from the clean training images, so we added color and blur augmentation.
submission.accomplishments: The model reaches 94 percent accuracy on our held-out split and the photo-to-diagnosis flow works end to end.
submission.what_we_learned: Validation accuracy on curated images overstates accuracy on real photos.
submission.whats_next: Collect real garden photos and add more crops.

controls.purpose: AI used only to write the code; no model in the product

submission.name: StudySprint
submission.tagline: A Pomodoro planner that turns your syllabus into focused sprints.
submission.inspiration: We kept losing track of what to study during long exam weeks.
submission.what_it_does: Students enter their courses and exam dates. StudySprint splits the remaining days into 25-minute sprints, shows a countdown timer and tracks completed sprints on a calendar.
submission.how_we_built_it: The app is React with a Firebase database. We used GitHub Copilot and ChatGPT to write most of our components and to debug our date logic.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Time zones broke our calendar until we stored every date in UTC.
submission.accomplishments: Course entry, sprint planning, the timer and the calendar all work.
submission.what_we_learned: AI coding assistants sped us up but we still had to understand every line.
submission.whats_next: Add reminders and shared study groups.

controls.purpose: Funny/goofy premise presented as life changing

submission.name: Snack Court
submission.tagline: Your fridge now holds a trial every time you open it after midnight.
submission.inspiration: We wanted to solve humanity's greatest crisis: eating cold pizza at 2 AM.
submission.what_it_does: When the fridge door sensor fires after midnight, Snack Court opens a dramatic courtroom on your phone. A cartoon judge reads the charges, your roommates vote guilty or not guilty within thirty seconds and the verdict sentences you to a punishment such as ten jumping jacks or a written apology to the pizza.
submission.how_we_built_it: A door sensor posts to a Node.js server, which pushes a Socket.IO event to every roommate's browser. The courtroom is a React page with hand-drawn sprites and a gavel sound effect; votes are tallied on the server.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Our first gavel sound was so loud it woke up a teammate's actual roommate.
submission.accomplishments: A full trial runs from fridge opening to verdict across three phones.
submission.what_we_learned: Comedy timing matters: the thirty-second vote window felt funnier than a minute.
submission.whats_next: An appeals court and a jury of strangers.

controls.purpose: Ordinary practical utility without a comic premise

submission.name: ParkSpot
submission.tagline: See open spaces in every campus garage before you drive in.
submission.inspiration: Students waste the first twenty minutes of class circling parking garages.
submission.what_it_does: ParkSpot shows a live count of open spaces per garage and level, predicts how full each garage will be in the next hour and sends a notification when your preferred garage is nearly full.
submission.how_we_built_it: We poll the university's public garage occupancy feed every minute, store counts in PostgreSQL and train a simple regression on the past month to predict the next hour. The front end is a React map.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The occupancy feed sometimes repeats stale values, so we detect and skip unchanged readings.
submission.accomplishments: Live counts, predictions and notifications work for all six garages.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned how to clean noisy sensor feeds.

controls.purpose: Financial-services workflow improvement without a proprietary BNY API

submission.name: BreakFinder
submission.tagline: Automatically match custodian and ledger trades and route settlement breaks.
submission.inspiration: A teammate interned in fund operations, where analysts reconciled trade files by hand every morning.
submission.what_it_does: Operations analysts upload the custodian's trade file and the internal ledger export. BreakFinder matches trades by identifier, quantity and settlement date, flags breaks such as quantity or price mismatches and assigns each break to an analyst queue with a suggested reason.
submission.how_we_built_it: A Python service parses both CSV formats with pandas, normalizes identifiers and runs exact then tolerance-based matching. Breaks are saved in PostgreSQL and shown in a React queue with filters by break type.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Partial fills split one ledger trade into several custodian rows, so we added aggregation before matching.
submission.accomplishments: Our synthetic 2,000-trade sample reconciles in under two seconds and every seeded break is flagged.
submission.what_we_learned: Most reconciliation work is data normalization rather than matching.
submission.whats_next: Support SWIFT message inputs and break aging reports.

controls.purpose: Central ElevenLabs integration that was not connected: fit high, functionality low

submission.name: Charla
submission.tagline: A Spanish conversation partner that talks back in a natural voice.
submission.inspiration: Language apps teach vocabulary, but we were scared of actually speaking.
submission.what_it_does: Charla is designed as a spoken Spanish conversation partner: you speak, it replies out loud in a natural ElevenLabs voice and corrects your grammar in the conversation. In the current demo, replies come from text and the voice plays from pre-recorded ElevenLabs clips.
submission.how_we_built_it: We planned a loop of browser speech recognition, a reply generator and the ElevenLabs streaming text-to-speech API. We generated twenty voice clips in the ElevenLabs dashboard; the live API call from our server is written but not connected.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Our streaming requests failed with authentication errors we could not fix in time, so the live voice loop does not work yet.
submission.accomplishments: The conversation screen and the pre-recorded voice replies work for one scripted dialogue.
submission.what_we_learned: We should have tested the voice API on the first night.
submission.whats_next: Connect the live ElevenLabs stream and add more scenarios.

controls.purpose: Central Databricks pipeline not connected to the product: fit high, functionality low

submission.name: FloodWatch
submission.tagline: Predict which Orlando streets flood next during a storm.
submission.inspiration: Our apartment complex floods every hurricane season with no warning.
submission.what_it_does: FloodWatch is meant to show a map of streets ranked by predicted flood risk for the next six hours. The current map shows predictions we exported once from Databricks; it does not update live.
submission.how_we_built_it: In Databricks we ingested NOAA rainfall and city 311 flooding reports into Delta tables, built features per street segment in a notebook and trained a gradient-boosted model tracked with MLflow. We did not finish connecting a serving endpoint to the web map.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Joining 311 reports to street segments took most of the weekend, and we ran out of time for model serving.
submission.accomplishments: The ingestion, feature and training notebooks run end to end in our workspace.
submission.what_we_learned: Spatial joins are harder than the model.
submission.whats_next: Deploy a model serving endpoint and refresh the map hourly.

controls.purpose: Sponsor tag and opt-in without any described sponsor use

submission.name: ShelfShare
submission.tagline: Lend and borrow textbooks with students in your dorm.
submission.inspiration: Textbooks are expensive and most sit unused after the semester.
submission.what_it_does: Students list textbooks they own, search their dorm's shelf and request a loan. The owner approves and both get a reminder before the return date.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used Next.js with a Supabase database and email reminders through Resend.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Handling overlapping loan requests took longer than expected.
submission.accomplishments: Listing, search, requests and reminders all work.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned row-level security in Supabase.

controls.purpose: Utility app with game-like rewards but no gameplay (field false positives: study, fitness and habit apps)

submission.name: FocusFern
submission.tagline: Grow a pixel fern by finishing your study tasks.
submission.inspiration: Our study group needed a nudge to actually start assignments.
submission.what_it_does: Students add study tasks with due dates and check them off when done. Each completed task earns coins that grow a pixel fern companion, daily streaks unlock new pot styles and a weekly leaderboard ranks friends in the same study group.
submission.how_we_built_it: A React app stores tasks and coin balances in Firebase. A scheduled function resets streaks at midnight and recomputes the leaderboard from completed tasks.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Streaks broke across time zones until we stored dates in UTC.
submission.accomplishments: Tasks, coins, fern growth, streaks and the leaderboard all work.
submission.what_we_learned: Small rewards made our own group finish more tasks during testing.

controls.purpose: Training game where play under rules is the main experience: must stay eligible

submission.name: Code Blue Drill
submission.tagline: Practice a campus emergency response before the clock runs out.
submission.inspiration: Our resident assistants freeze during their first real emergency.
submission.what_it_does: Players act as a resident assistant during a timed emergency scenario. Each turn reveals a new event, and the player picks one of three actions such as calling dispatch, clearing a hallway or checking a room. Wrong or slow choices cost points, and the round is lost if the timer runs out before the building is safe. A final score ranks each attempt.
submission.how_we_built_it: We built it in Godot with a branching event graph, a countdown timer, a scoring system for each action and three scenario levels of increasing difficulty.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Balancing the timer so the hardest level was tense but winnable took many playtests.
submission.accomplishments: All three scenarios are playable from the menu through the win or loss screen.
submission.what_we_learned: Clear feedback after each choice mattered more than graphics.
submission.whats_next: More scenarios and a two-player mode.

controls.purpose: Sponsor use described as small, optional and outside the core flow (field weak-fit false positives)

submission.name: FridgeMap
submission.tagline: Find community fridges and pantries near campus.
submission.inspiration: Students facing food insecurity did not know where free food was available.
submission.what_it_does: FridgeMap shows community fridges and food pantries on a map with opening hours and user-reported stock levels. Users can report when a fridge is restocked or empty. An optional Gemini button writes a one-line summary of a selected location; the map, listings and reports are the core.
submission.how_we_built_it: A Next.js map uses Leaflet and a PostgreSQL table of locations from the county open-data portal. Stock reports update each location in real time. The optional summary button sends the location's listing text to the Gemini API.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Open-data addresses were messy, so we geocoded and cleaned them by hand.
submission.accomplishments: The map, listings and live stock reports work for 40 locations.
submission.what_we_learned: Real-time reports only help if enough people submit them.

controls.purpose: Sponsor performs a meaningful step in the main flow but is not the centre: must stay eligible

submission.name: LabNote
submission.tagline: Turn messy lab notebook photos into searchable experiment records.
submission.inspiration: Our chemistry lab loses results in handwritten notebooks.
submission.what_it_does: Students photograph a notebook page. The app extracts the procedure, measurements and results into a structured record, and lab members search records by reagent or date. Gemini reads each photo and returns the structured fields; the search index, record editor and lab sharing are built around those records.
submission.how_we_built_it: A Flask backend sends each uploaded photo to the Gemini API with a JSON schema for procedure, measurements and results, validates the response, then stores records in SQLite with a full-text index. A React front end handles upload, review and search.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Gemini sometimes merged two measurements, so users review and correct each record before saving.
submission.accomplishments: Photo to reviewed, searchable record works end to end on our own notebook pages.
submission.what_we_learned: A review step made extraction errors acceptable.
submission.whats_next: Unit normalization and export to the lab's spreadsheet.
